verses.text: Then hateful Strife gave birth to painful Toil,
Forgetfulness and Hunger, and Sorrows that bring tears;
Clashes and Battles, Murders and Slaughter;
Quarrels, lying Words and Arguments;
Lawlessness and Ruin, always close companions;
and Oath, who brings the worst suffering to people on earth
whenever someone knowingly swears a false oath.
Pontus, the Sea, fathered Nereus, truthful and free from lies,
the eldest of his children. They call him the Old Man
because he is trustworthy and gentle, and never forgets
what is right, but has thoughts that are fair and kind.
Pontus also fathered mighty Thaumas and proud Phorcys
by mating with Gaia, the Earth, and Ceto with her lovely cheeks,
and Eurybia, whose heart is as hard as unbreakable stone.
Nereus had dearly loved daughters, all goddesses,
in the sea that yields no harvest, with lovely-haired Doris,
daughter of Oceanus, the great river:
Ploto, Eucrante, Sao and Amphitrite;
Eudora, Thetis, Galene and Glauce;
Cymothoe, Speio, Thoe and lovely Halia;
Pasithea, Erato and Eunice with her rosy arms;
graceful Melite, Eulimene and Agave;
Doto, Proto, Pherusa and Dynamene;
Nesaea, Actaea and Protomedea;
Doris, Panopea and beautiful Galatea;
lovely Hippothoe and Hipponoe with her rosy arms;
and Cymodoce, who calms the waves on the misty sea
and the blasts of raging winds, with Cymatolege
and Amphitrite of the lovely ankles, doing so with ease;
Cymo, Eione and Halimede with her lovely crown;
Glauconome, who loves to smile, and Pontoporea;
Leagora, Euagora and Laomedea;
Polynoe, Autonoe and Lysianassa;
Euarne, lovely in figure and flawless in looks;
Psamathe with her graceful body, and glorious Menippe;
Neso, Eupompe, Themisto and Pronoe;
and Nemertes, who has her immortal father’s mind.
These daughters were born to faultless Nereus,
fifty in all, and all knew how to do their work without fault.
Thaumas married the daughter of deep-flowing Oceanus,
Electra, who gave birth to swift Iris
and the lovely-haired Harpies, Aello and Ocypete,
who keep pace with gusts of wind and birds
on their swift wings, darting high through the air.
Ceto bore Phorcys the fair-cheeked Graiae,
gray-haired from birth, whom they call the Graiae, the Old Women,
both the immortal gods and humans who walk the earth:
Pemphredo in her beautiful robe and Enyo in her saffron-yellow robe.
Ceto also bore the Gorgons, who live beyond famous Oceanus,
at the world’s far edge toward Night, where the clear-voiced Hesperides live:
Sthenno, Euryale and Medusa, who suffered a terrible fate.
Medusa was mortal; the others were immortal and ageless,
both of them. Dark-haired Poseidon lay with Medusa
in a soft meadow among spring flowers.
When Perseus cut off Medusa’s head,
great Chrysaor and the horse Pegasus sprang out.
Pegasus took his name from the springs of Oceanus, where
he was born; Chrysaor was named for the golden sword he held in his hands.
Pegasus flew away, leaving the earth, mother of flocks,
and reached the immortal gods. He lives in Zeus’s halls,
carrying thunder and lightning for Zeus, the wise planner.
